I thought it might be useful to summarize what has been said in a number of posts in this section around what would be interesting to read in a new post on lean autoformalization. Hope other find it useful and add/remove items (this is a currently a one person preference, but maybe other agree).

What is not interesting:

  • off-the-shelf frontier models (ChatGPT, Claude, etc) are capable of autoformalizing a lot of previously unformalized pieces of informal math proofs given enough time and resources, if one doesn't care about the quality of the formalization (proof quality and definition architecture) and further reuse and maintainability. So solely a binary positive results like - I asked Claude to formalize a well-known proof given an informal argument and it succeeded (meaning solely it was checked by lean) by itself is not of great interest.

What is interesting:

  • autoformalization of a previously open question - though the informal AI solution finding (which seems to right now often proceed formalization) is probably the interesting part, while the autoformalization that follows can be almost trivial by itself (but important for a quicker proof acceptance maybe).
  • analysis of the quality of the autoformalization - note this is subjective, and probably currently requires a human lean expertise. Current set of lean experts is small and most are quite busy, asking them to spend time to evaluate the quality of the autoformalization is unlikely to be successful.
  • analysis of the checking time of the formalization output - the same result can be formalized in vastly faster or slower to check ways.
  • autoformalizing libraries - autoformalizing that had to make non-trivial (and not regurgitating existing in mathlib) architectural decisions that would further aid downstream formalization.
  • analysis of the engineering methods and costs - models used, custom harnesses, tokens, time, etc. involved to achieve the formalization. Comparisons between custom harnesses and say generic ones like Claude code or Codex. Techniques for minimizing cost.
  • semi-autoformalization comparisons - fully autonomous process achieved quality or time X, while with human steering (Y hours or specific inputs) some measurable improvement was achieved.
  • failed autoformalizations due to real errors - formalization failing for valid reasons that were missed in informal proof.
  • failed autoformalizations due to surprising lean' foundations limitations - I don't know much about this, but seems possible for results that have to do with math foundations?
  • misformalizations - an autoformalization that was found to be subtly incorrect and how the process was strengthened
  • producing new lean companions like https://github.com/teorth/analysis that are meant to be read and play-tested by other people.

I think the following are good examples:

  • https://frenzymath.com/blog/conjecture/
  • https://github.com/Vilin97/Clawristotle/blob/landau/TECHNICAL_REPORT.md
  • ... add more

Rado Kirov said:

  • off-the-shelf frontier models (ChatGPT, Claude, etc) are fully capable of autoformalizing almost any piece of informal math proofs given enough time and resources. So solely a binary positive results like - I asked Claude to formalize a well-known proof given an informal argument and it succeeded by itself is not of great interest.

Woah, this is wildly untrue. If you add some very strong caveats about "and all the interesting design work for prerequisites has already been done and is available in Mathlib", then sure, yes. But as stated, this is wrong.

There is just zero evidence at this point that you can take textbooks A and B, where B depends on substantial material from A, autoformalize A for $1000, and obtain a result which is not just accurately reflecting the content of A, and valid Lean, but actually usable to then continue autoformalization of B.
That would be an awesome benchmark (even with smaller sized chunks of mathematics).

very interesting, happy to adjust it to reflect a more wider opinion. I must be biased because my own experiments have been on math that doesn't need heavy architectural design work on top of mathlib and it has been extremely successful (with the usual quality caveats).

Also from what I see posted here there are no negative results (survivor bias?) and clear uptick in successes. Separately, quality of formalization is hard to evaluate and requires deeper lean expertise to do so (which I did call out as area of interest).

Thinking by analogy with regular software development, if someone goes to python forums to just show I build an app with AI, everyone will just shrug (which is basically what is happening here too). At this point it is basically accepted "AI can write code". Of course there are tons of caveats around quality in the small (code quality) and in the large (code architecture). Unlike binary outcomes like the code was written and runs (checks in the proof world), those are subjective measures which makes it hard to get an agreement.

I think a few months back there was a bit of open question, can frontier models write lean given the training corpus is smaller, and I think that part can be put to rest. They are fully capable of writing lean proof code if 1) given a informal scaffold for the proof (known results) 2) put aside question of code quality 3) put aside question of code architecture.
editted above to call out more explicitly caveat about "not caring about quality" in "not interesting" and a new item autoformalizing libraries in interesting.

There is just zero evidence at this point that you can take textbooks A and B, where B depends on substantial material from A, autoformalize A for $1000, and obtain a result which is not just accurately reflecting the content of A, and valid Lean, but actually usable to then continue autoformalization of B.

That would be an awesome benchmark (even with smaller sized chunks of mathematics).

+1 could be interesting to pose a direct challenge, as a way to steer all those tokens spent towards something the larger community can use better. Ultimately the goal would be to get more things in mathlib, but for now AI generated "good architecture" lean libraries can still be build outside, but with more explicit goals toward reusuable and maintainable (subtly different and just as hard to pin down) code.

I would be interested to see "bad architecture" autoformalaztion examples - i.e. places where the formalization of A succeed but it was clearly unusable for B because the definitions were wrong in some way, i.e. you got a correct formal proof but you don't have a library.

Is say Munkres -> Hatcher a good example of A -> B? As an aside I just saw a paper of autoformalizing Munkres in Isabelle, and to my earlier point, I believe something like that can be trivially reproduced in Lean, but the question whether the formalization is good enough to reuse for the next book is quite interesting.

I think that we need to speak very carefully when talking about things like "AI can write lean code given an informal scaffold". I think the reality is far more nuanced.

Right now we have never seen an AI autonomously make a complex definition and then make API for it. We see them using complex definitions in mathlib. We see them making definitions autonomously when they are only a few lines long. But what a lot of people seem to be failing to understand right now is that what is being autoformalised is not really representative of what is actually going on in mathematics, it is only representative of the small corner where complex definitions which are not already in mathlib are not needed. I think that part of the problem is that professional mathematicians are not standing up and saying "try this paper", what is happening instead is that tech companies and individuals are saying "I've achieved this goal which I chose myself" and people are jumping to conclusions.

As I have said many times before, all known proofs of Fermat's last theorem need Mazur's theorem that the torsion subgroup of an elliptic curve over Q has size at most 16. This is a 150 page paper of Mazur from 1977 which is very clearly written and has been revisited numerous times in the literature. I claim that current systems are a very long way away from formalising this paper and trust me there are far more technical results than Mazur which need to be done before FLT. The problem with the paper is that it uses existence and basic properties of integral models of modular curves and that mathlib cannot even state these properties right now.

To give you another example of how far autoformalisation is from reality, I claim that the percentage of papers published in the Annals of mathematics in this decade whose statements can be formalised in lean using mathlib without making any new definitions is about 10% and that many of the missing definitions are technical and would be nontrivial projects which would take a human between an afternoon and several months of full time work to formalise (or in a few cases several years). Theorems built on these definitions are not autoformalisable with current techniques. Machines are not ready and the deluge of successes is misleading because it's the companies not the community choosing the goals.

Another thing which might become an issue but which isn't really talked about because people are just hoping that it will go away is issues of slowdowns and timeouts. We regularly see AI switching off or hugely increasing timeout limits and this is for code where experts don't need to do this. But there are places in mathlib where even the experts are facing slowdowns because of complex and subtle issues involving universes or typeclass inference which the core team are not working on. Algebraic geometry might just grind to a halt one day and we are still only up to about 1962. Mazur's paper (which uses a lot of algebraic geometry) is 1977. Can either humans or AI get that far? Maybe one day. But I don't think we can do it today.

big +1 proof performance is a huge thing that people are missing with the autoformalization efforts and might be a good proxy for proof quality (I believe well-factored proofs are both more readable, maintainable and faster to typecheck). Added to the list above.

The "A → B" book dependency question seems to follow from "AI can autoformalize any book", since we can concatenate A and B to create a new book AB and then autoformalize it. And OTOH books obviously have dependencies inside themselves. So while I understand the intent of the challenge (when the super basic API sucks, the nontrivial theorems are a pain to prove), I don't think framing it as book dependencies pinpoints the issue and it might lead to people claiming they've done it even if the core problem isn't solved. Maybe the book framing works if we require more hops "A → B → C → D" (much like Kevin keeping track of publication years) since the issue is likely to come up when the dependency material (from A) is considered trivial (in D).
I think we should be more precise when saying what AI can't currently do, since people/companies exploit (not intentionally) minor inaccuracies in those, then it looks like we're moving the goalpost and that there was some progress, but actually we just clarified the goal and the goalpost didn't move.

agree, A -> B is a proxy for quality of the code architecture for A, but if one doesn't care about the quality of B either, it is not that great.

I think the underlying problem is that the number of people that are willing to experiment with AI formalization greatly outnumbers the ones that can speak about the quality of the lean architecture.

I think that part of the problem is that professional mathematicians are not standing up and saying "try this paper", what is happening instead is that tech companies and individuals are saying "I've achieved this goal which I chose myself" and people are jumping to conclusions.

This makes sense to me, posing more challenges - places where noone knows how to even do the lean definitions (maybe the underlying informal math architecture is subtly lacking/broken?)

Ultimately, the AI people want no-human-in-the-loop benchmarks to hill-climb against, which makes the actual things needed - high-quality lean math libraries very non-appealing to them.

Rado Kirov said:

but if one doesn't care about the quality of B either

That's not what I meant (nor what I believe Kim meant). The question is whether it's even possible, not what the quality is: i.e. what happens when the poor quality of the previous code makes it impossible to progress through the current proof (without completely rewriting the dependency to specifically fit the current proof), aka "the poor quality catches up to the LLM".

The question is whether it's even possible, not what the quality is: i.e. what happens when the poor quality of the previous code makes it impossible to progress through the current proof

Interesting, basically I haven't seen AI formalization get completely stuck, but I have seen it produce messier and slower proofs. This is my own problem because I only poked at undergraduate mathematics, which greatly benefits from mathlib's definitions.

I was going to ask for a minimal example of such autoformalization blockage. Kevin's Mazur paper is one (thanks for sharing it!). But then it is also dawning on me that the current high-interest PR environment from AI companies, makes every be very careful when posing challenges, so that results are not misrepresented or completed in bad faith.

If not clear, I am not affiliated with any AI company, just a someone who likes math and likes computers, and very excited about a future where more and more of the proofs are checked by the computer.

Btw, this situation is completely mirrored in the larger Math <> AI conversation (using AI for math progress outside formalization) and same challenges happening there. https://1stproof.org/ was the more careful thoughtful challenge posed, not sure whether it achieved its goals, I can imagine something like that for autoformalization.

What about posing the classification of finite simple groups (CFSG) as a challenge? One advantage is that the GLS project has been very clear about what prerequisites they rely on (one of them being of course Feit-Thompson, which is already a known success story for human formalization). For something like Mazur's theorem, it's not immediately clear what the prerequisites are, so it's harder to assess partial progress. Also, there is a well-defined series of books that can be used to assess the "book A -> book B" issue mentioned earlier.

Autoformalizing the CFSG is something which I imagine that enthusiasts would say is already a solved problem (someone just has to pay for it), but which I suspect is not, even though it is a relatively self-contained corner of mathematics. And if its autoformalization is a solved problem and someone solves it, the result would be of benefit to the mathematical community, since there are still some people around who don't entirely trust the proof.

By the way, the GLS project isn't quite complete. Ten volumes have appeared so far; the list of prerequisites (which includes Aschbacher-Smith) was increased mid-project and could in principle increase again, but probably won't. I asked Ron Solomon in January 2025 for an update, and here is what he said:

Many thanks for your interest in our project.  I have been consistently overoptimistic concerning the timeline for completion of my work with Richard Lyons.  Volume 11 has been the most challenging for us, as we attempt to extend two difficult papers of Michael Aschbacher under somewhat weaker hypotheses.  Nevertheless, I think our work is going well and I currently hope that we will be able to submit Volume 11 for publication by the AMS this calendar year.  There will be at least two additional volumes after Volume 11.  The good news is that Gernot Stroth has sent us an 800-page typescript destined to serve as the principal contents of the remaining volumes. However a “bridge” is required between the conclusion of Volume 11 and Stroth’s manuscript.  This is not unprecedented.  A similar bridge was needed in the original set of classification papers, and was provided in a joint paper of Aschbacher, Gorenstein and Lyons.  Again, this paper will have to be extended a bit.  Given that there are 26 sporadic simple groups, it would be numerologically satisfying if our work could be completed in 13 volumes and in the year ’26.  We shall see.

One other clarifying comment. Several of the prerequisites listed by GLS are group theory textbooks/research monographs that weren't written with GLS in mind. So when I referred to the "book A -> book B" issue, I had in mind not just the "official volumes" of the GLS project, but the leap from these background-material textbooks to the GLS project. It's quite common for research papers and monographs to say something like, "The first five chapters of Textbook X contain more than enough background for what we need here," and it would be interesting to see whether autoformalizers agree, or whether they complain about yawning gaps not covered by Textbook X.

I think that before thinking about the classification one could ask the much much easier question of whether the odd order theorem can be autoformalised given that there's a good informal explanation of it and a formalisation in Rocq! And then also the much much easier question of autoformalisation of the Aschbacher--Smith prerequisite quasi-thin stuff. But I totally agree that the classification is a great long-term target and thanks a lot for the update.

I think there are sociological advantages to designating the CFSG as a whole, rather than some specific piece of it.

First of all, even though you and I might laugh at autoformalizing CFSG, perhaps Math, Inc. won't, so it gives them the opportunity to go on record as claiming that autoformalizing CFSG is easy (or at least not laughable) and then having to put up or shut up.

Secondly, if we peel off some piece of it, such as the odd order theorem, and the AI companies succeed, then I guarantee that someone is going to say, "Oh, well, that's not interesting, because the odd order theorem was already formalized." Or maybe someone will complain that the AI company cherry-picked some low-hanging fruit. Even if the person proposing the odd order theorem is not the same as the person who pooh-poohs it after the fact, it's going to come off as goalpost-moving. It's much less likely that people will say, "Oh, you autoformalized CFSG? Yawn. Wake me up when you autoformalize something interesting."

Thirdly, even if, as you and I suspect, autoformalizing all of CFSG is unrealistic right now, I expect that there are nontrivial portions of it that are within reach. I don't know which portions those might be, and I think it's fair to give the AI companies some options to pick feasible targets within the larger target. This gives them a better framework for claiming partial success without getting brushed off as simply cherry-picking.

Even just the Odd-Order Theorem in Lean.
Or intermediate: all the assumed prerequisites that the 2nd Generation CFSG has named. A lot of that is standard group theory that Mathlib just needs

If autoformalisation of background material that's considered standard in the theory of finite groups is of such low quality the subsequent autoformalisation of real serious theorems using it grinds into the ground..... Well, I think that proves the claim by yourself and others that current AI tools can't get the foundational definitions and API right. If it does get it in a workable place, then an interesting discussion can be opened up.

Let me say a little more about the background results assumed by GLS, since I think most people don't know much about it. The discussion begins on page 46 of Volume 1. They begin by outright assuming the construction, and some basic properties, of twenty-six sporadic groups (they say "the" twenty-six sporadic groups, but of course, they're not assuming that there aren't any others).

We shall simply assume here that the twenty-six sporadic groups exist, and each of them (except M11M_{11}M11​) is uniquely determined up to isomorphism as the only simple group with its centralizer of involution pattern.

They then give a long list background references. I won't give them all here, but here are the basic group-theory references. Only the first two are really fundamental; most of the others are needed only for certain specific results.

  1. Aschbacher, Finite Group Theory.
  2. Gorenstein, Finite Groups.
  3. Huppert, Endliche Gruppen I.
  4. Huppert and Blackburn, Finite Groups III.
  5. Suzuki, Group Theory I, II.
  6. Feit, The Representation Theory of Finite Groups.
  7. Isaacs, Character Theory of Finite Groups.
  8. Carter, Finite Groups of Lie Type.
  9. Dieudonne, La geometrie des groupes classiques.
  10. Steinberg, Lectures on Chevalley Groups.
  11. Steinberg, Endomorphisms of Linear Algebraic Groups.
  12. Aschbacher, Sporadic Groups.
  13. Gorenstein and Lyons, The local structure of finite groups of characteristic 2 type.

After that comes a list of fifteen advanced papers/monographs, which I won't list explicitly. These include "revisions of certain portions of the classification proof" and papers on specific topics, e.g., the odd-order theorem, the recognition of split (B,N)-pairs of rank 1, signalizer functor theorems, and Brauer's papers on modular character theory. The total page count of these 15 references is close to 1000.
In Volume 8, they add four more references.

  1. L. E. Dickson's classification of smallest-dimensional faithful modules for the symmetric groups.
  2. J. McLaughlin's characterization of groups generated by transvections on a finite vector space of odd order.
  3. R. Gramlich's exposition of the state of Phan theory.
  4. Theorems of R. Blok, C. Hoffman, and S. Shpectorov on amalgames of Curtis-Tits and Phan types.

In Volume 9, they say they add "two books by Aschbacher" (although curiously, one of them is "Sporadic Groups" which was already listed in Volume 1; the other is "3-Transposition Groups") and "two papers, one by Segev on the Baby Monster, and one by Griess, Meierfrankenfeld and Segev, on the Monster." Then they mention the two Aschbacher-Smith volumes. Finally, in Volume 10, they need a specific result from the Atlas.

I said earlier that I think it's unlikely that the list of background results will be expanded, but this exercise of typing up the details makes me less sure. It would not surprise me if a couple of other papers are tacked on to the list when the remaining volumes are published.

My friends in Tsinghua University have received emails about this project. I haven't found public announcements on the website yet, perhaps it's only for internal now.

It's about autoformalising Munkres' book on topology in Isabelle/HOL, but I think one important takeway the authors note is this

The proofs are therefore sound, but the definitions are less reusable than they could be—a user inheriting these definitions without the accompanying assumptions could derive spurious results. This pattern is characteristic of LLM-generated code: the model reliably produces definitions that are sufficient for the proofs at hand but does not anticipate downstream reuse or defensive design.

source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.07455

@Jz Pan that sounds like the kind of thing that would be done on the quiet, and then announced with a big splash for publicity purposes (I'm thinking other reasons too, but I'll keep those to myself).

@Timothy Chow thanks for that! From the discussions you and I have had, wiring in the big manuscript of Stroth as the last volume (or two volumes) of the project might conceivably need some extra prerequisites.

The proofs are therefore sound, but the definitions are less reusable than they could be—a user inheriting these definitions without the accompanying assumptions could derive spurious results.

This is very interesting, I should read the paper more carefully. The example they provides is

The formalization defines is_topology_on X T without requiring T ⊆ P(X). This omission is not merely cosmetic: one can formally derive, for instance, that the collection T := {∅, {0}, {1}, {0, 1}} satisfies is_topology_on {0} T, despite containing {1} ̸⊆ {0}

I don't know Isabelle, but I am guessing it untyped like Python. I was wondering if this should classified as 1) human text is loose with types or 2) the formalization agent messed the translation (partially because the formalization language allows for more flexibility)

looking up the exact text in Munkres - Definition. A topology on a set X is a collection T of subsets of X having the following properties:, feels like more of 2).

I don't know Isabelle either, but I was under the impression that its foundations were based on set theory - so, no types, hence the absence of typing information in the statements.

But, I'm also surprised that the autoformalisation is pronounced sound with this slip in the definition of a topology (and of course, the text in the book does mention that the sets in T must be subsets of X, so the sloppiness is in the translation, not the original text). I don't have an example in mind, but I would expect that some standard theorems would become false with such a definition (unless of course each later theorem statement added the missing condition).
Isabelle/HOL is based on Church’s simple type theory.

Isabelle itself is a rather general framework, so you'll often see people talk about not just Isabelle but Isabelle-slash-something, such as Isabelle/HOL or Isabelle/ZF. You probably formed your impression about set theory because you heard someone talking about Isabelle/ZF. But as Kevin said, Isabelle/HOL is based on simple type theory. Isabelle does avoid dependent types; that's by design, since Larry Paulson has argued that dependent types add unnecessary complexity.

I got it running recently on linux (it might be harder to get it running on other operating systems, not sure) by following the instructions on the Archon README here. These guys claimed to prove a conjecture in commutative algebra and have made it extremely easy to install and run comparator to verify that their proof is OK.

FWIW I did have one problem which was diagnosed and solved here #lean4 > comparator @ 💬

@Emily Riehl Since you asked about other tools, besides Comparator there are external checkers (Lean's official solution in some sense and a component of Comparator) and SafeVerify. Also, while Comparator is really good at checking theorems if someone trustworthy wrote the theorem, it is less good if the statement of the theorem is itself long and complicated and written by a human/AI which you don't trust.

And on the topic of autoformalizion and comparator, I think it is still a bit of an open problem how to verify that definitions are correct especially if long. If they are small you can read them, but I think a lot can be done with proving that definitions satisfy various known essential properties (including if possible existence/uniqueness properties or universal properties). Long before AI was a big thing, the Liquid Tensor Experiment used a similar approach to verify that their definitions were correct (and that they didn't accidently prove a trivial result). That approach is probably compatible with something like Comparator.

How would one scale heavy computational proofs without kernel timeouts or unverified native_decide? Separately, how would one prevent generated proofs from becoming isolated formalizations that create technical debt rather than reusable infrastructure?
